analysis.one_liner: Converts Social Security into mandatory private investment accounts and trims guaranteed benefits.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a hearing or a vote; it died in committee with zero cosponsors.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would rebuild Social Security around personal investment accounts. Everyone born in 1986 or later would automatically have their full 6.2% employee payroll contribution put into an individual account invested in stocks and bonds instead of into the traditional pension; workers born between 1953 and 1986 could choose to opt in. At retirement, participants would draw the money as an annuity bought from insurance companies approved by a new federal board, or as scheduled withdrawals. People who stayed in the traditional system would see their benefits grow more slowly, because the bill switches benefit formulas from wage indexing to inflation (CPI) indexing. It also creates a new federal Individual Investment Board to run the program and directs the Treasury to top up the trust funds from general tax revenue.
analysis.who_benefits: If it had passed, the largest beneficiaries would have been the financial industry: every participant's 6.2% payroll contribution would flow through professional asset managers chosen by the new Individual Investment Board, with commission and administrative fees charged against balances, and every retiree taking an annuity would have to buy it from an insurer certified and approved by the Board. Tier III self-directed accounts could be held only at banks, insured credit unions, or regulated investment companies. Workers who elected the accounts (and everyone born after 1985, who would have no choice) would own real, inheritable property and could benefit if markets performed well, with a poverty-level minimum benefit as a floor and tax-free treatment of accounts and annuity payments.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Asset managers, annuity insurers, and account holders

how_it_helps.text: Participants would own their balances as property, could leave them to heirs in a lump sum at death, and could not have them garnished or assigned — something current Social Security benefits do not offer.

Workers born between 1953 and 1986 could elect in voluntarily; only those born in 1986 or later would be enrolled automatically, with 100% of their redirected 6.2% contribution deposited to their account.

Money would first sit in a safe Tier I fund, then move to a diversified Tier II fund with a 60% stock / 40% bond default, and participants with over $10,000 could direct funds into self-directed Tier III accounts.

Participants could begin drawing their account early once it could buy an annuity paying at least the poverty line, and a supplemental minimum benefit payment would top up accounts that fall short of a poverty-level annuity at retirement.
Account funds, recognition bonds, and annuity payments would be excluded from taxable income.

analysis.who_pays: Workers born in 1986 or later would be enrolled automatically and would bear market risk on their entire retirement contribution, with fees deducted along the way and a backstop set only at the poverty line. Workers who stayed in the traditional system — and all current and future beneficiaries outside disability — would see guaranteed benefits grow more slowly under CPI indexing. All taxpayers would bear the transition cost, since the bill appropriates general Treasury funds to keep the trust funds at adequate balances and pays supplemental minimum benefits out of the general fund.
analysis.who_pays_short: Younger workers, traditional beneficiaries, and taxpayers

drawbacks.text: Workers whose accounts performed poorly near retirement would face lower lifetime income; the only backstop is a supplemental payment topping accounts up to a poverty-level annuity, and that floor is reduced dollar-for-dollar by any other need-based cash benefits the participant receives.

The bill cuts benefits in the traditional system too, replacing wage indexing with CPI indexing for non-disability beneficiaries — a slower growth formula that reduces guaranteed benefits over time for people who never open an account.

Administrative and commission fees would be charged against participants' balances, and the bill requires disclosure of them, acknowledging they are a real cost; account balances also bear investment losses, unlike the current defined benefit.
Financing the transition is left to the general Treasury, which must appropriate whatever sums are needed to keep the trust funds at adequate balances — a cost borne by all taxpayers.

The strongest good-faith case for the bill: personal accounts would be property participants own and can leave to heirs, unlike current benefits, and long-run stock returns historically exceed the implicit return of the pay-as-you-go system. The bill also tries to limit risk with a conservative default and a poverty-level minimum benefit.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The genuine upside is ownership: participants would hold real, inheritable assets instead of a statutory promise, could opt in if born before 1986, and could retire early once their accounts could fund a poverty-level annuity. The costs are substantial and concentrated on those with the least margin for error. Redirecting the full 6.2% contribution away from the pooled system shrinks guaranteed benefits; the CPI re-indexing cuts them further for everyone else; participants who retire into a market downturn lock in lower annuities for life; fees skim balances every year; and the poverty-line floor is eroded by dollar-for-dollar offsets against other need-based benefits. The bill also shifts the financing risk to the general Treasury, which must top up the trust funds. Taken together, the design transfers retirement risk from the government to individuals while creating a large fee-paying customer base for the financial industry, and it died without a single cosponsor from either party.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee and its Social Security Subcommittee in April 2007, and with no cosponsors and no scheduled action it sat there until the Congress ended in January 2009.

narrative.text: Sam Johnson introduced the bill on April 23, 2007; the same day it was referred to the House Committee on Ways and Means.
Two days later it was referred to the Subcommittee on Social Security, and no further action — no hearing, no markup, no vote — was ever taken.
Not a single member of either party signed on as a cosponsor.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Working people who would have been enrolled in the accounts or had their guaranteed benefits trimmed by the CPI change are better off that it died, since no one gained anything from the bill's demise. The asset management and insurance industries simply forwent a potential new market.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Workers whose guaranteed benefits stayed untouched

for.name: Rep. Sam Johnson
for.what_they_did: Sole sponsor; introduced the bill on April 23, 2007 and never attracted a cosponsor.

against.name: Charles Rangel
against.role: Chair, House Ways and Means Committee
against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill before the committee; after its referral to the Social Security Subcommittee, no hearing, markup, or vote was ever scheduled.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken, so no party split can be measured; the only evidence is that a single Republican sponsored it and zero members of either party cosponsored it.

industries.note: The bill redirects every participant's 6.2% payroll contribution through professional asset managers and Board-selected investment funds, with commission and administrative fees charged against balances. It converts a pay-as-you-go public program into a permanent, mandatory fee-paying customer base for the industry.

Retirees could take their account only as an annuity bought from issuers the Individual Investment Board certifies and approves, guaranteeing insurers a stream of new customers. The annuity cost comes out of the worker's own account balance.

industries.industry: Banks, credit unions, and regulated investment companies
industries.note: Only these institutions could serve as trustees of Tier III self-directed accounts, giving them a privileged role in the new system. Their compensation would come out of workers' accounts.

industries.industry: Traditional Social Security beneficiaries and the trust funds
industries.note: The bill credits participants' wages only under the new account part (except for disability), shrinking the covered earnings base, and switches benefit growth from wage indexing to CPI indexing for non-disability beneficiaries, reducing future benefits. The general Treasury must then appropriate whatever is needed to keep the trust funds solvent.
